attributes.title: Level 6

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create an array to store the image variables?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbols should be used to contain and separate the elements in an array?

❓ What background color might be used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that elements in an array should be contained by a pair of brackets and each element should be separated by a comma.
steps.instructions:
Set up the project by creating  an image variable array and setting the background color!


Notice that there is already code in the editor to create Person and Ninja sprite kinds, store image variables, and to organize the project code.


Under the image variable code, use the keyword let to declare a new array called personList. Type an assignment operator and a pair of brackets [ ] with the names of the image variables inside, separated by commas. 


Set a background color for the project. Open Scene and drag [set background color to (color)] underneath // game set up. Type a value inside the parentheses to set a background color.


Click ▶ to see the background color displayed on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a function with a number parameter, and use /** to create documentation for the callLevel function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What symbols are used to create a documentation box comment?

❓ Why does the parameter type need to be declared inside the parentheses of the function definition?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that using /** and */ to contain a comment helps the coder understand and remember the purpose of different custom functions in a project. This is especially helpful when a function is called in a different place than the function is defined; it provides an easy way to remember what the function’s code will do.

💡Point out to the ninja that when adding parameters to a function, the type must be defined. Parameters can accept number, string, sprite, image, or Boolean arguments. In this example, the numOfPeople parameter will accept a number argument, which will be used to spawn Person sprites.
steps.instructions:
Create a function that will call a new level that contains multiple sprites!


Click Advanced, then open Functions and drag [function doSomething] underneath // function set up. 


Name the function callLevel then add a parameter to set how many Person sprites will appear on screen in the level. Inside the function’s parentheses, type the parameter name numOfPeople and a colon :, then set the type to number. 


Above the callLevel function definition, type /** then notice the MakeCode editor automatically ends the documentation comment with */. Between the asterisks * write a brief description of how the callLevel function will spawn Ninja and Person sprites depending on the difficulty level.

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace img`...` with the Ninja image variable name in sprites.create?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the Ninja sprite be used for in this project? 

❓ Did you set the Ninja sprite to appear in a random position?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In this project, the user will have to find the Ninja sprite, which will be hidden amongst Person sprites on screen. It’s important that the Ninja sprite is set to a random position, so that its position changes each time the project is played.
steps.instructions:
Use the function to create a single Ninja sprite!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets of the callLevel function. Update the sprite name, then replace img`...` with the ninjaImage variable name. Update the sprite kind to Ninja.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under sprites.create. Update the sprite name, then use randint to place the Ninja sprite in a random position on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the run condition so that the loop continues to run as long as the counter variable is less than numOfPeople?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓How many times will the for loop run when the callLevel function is called?

❓Which images will be used for each Person sprite created? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the callLevel function is called, 1 Ninja sprite will be created and a variety of Person sprites will be spawned, based on the argument used in the callLevel function call. 

💡 Remind the ninja that there are 3 images in the personList array. Each time a Person sprite is created, 1 of the 3 images (indexes 0-2) is selected to be used as the Person sprite’s image.
steps.instructions:
Use a loop inside the function to create multiple Person sprites!


Open Loops and drag [for] inside the curly brackets of the callLevel function. Update the run condition so that the loop runs as long as i is less than the value of the numOfPeople parameter.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Update the sprite name, then replace img`...` with personList and a pair of brackets [ ]. Inside the brackets [ ], use randint to select a random value from the array between 0 and the 2. Update the sprite kind to Person.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under sprites.create. Update the sprite name, then use randint to place each Person sprite in a random position on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use commas to separate the three strings in the choice parameters of showPlayerChoices?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the Story extension be used for in this project?

❓ What does the showPlayerChoices function do? How might it be used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has selected the arcade-storytelling extension to the project and the Story menu is available in the editor.

💡 The showPlayerChoices function shows a menu of choices to the user and pauses the project until the user selects a choice. This function can be useful for creating different stories in a project or modifying parameters, such as the level of challenge, based on the user’s choice.
steps.instructions:
Use the Story extension to create different levels of difficulty that the user can choose from! 


Add the Story extension by clicking More then selecting Extensions. Scroll down then select the arcade-storytelling extension to add it to the project.


Open Story, drag [show player choices (choice1) (choice2)] under // game set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

story.showPlayerChoices("", "")

The showPlayerChoices function takes multiple parameters: multiple user choices. Update the choices by typing “Easy”, “Hard”, and “Impossible” inside the parentheses, separated by commas.


Click ▶ to see the menu of 3 possible choices presented to the user!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a checkLastAnswer inside the if and else if conditions to check the user’s choice?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the checkLastAnswer function do? How is it used?

❓ How does the user’s choice change what happens in the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The checkLastAnswer function checks the last answer submitted by the user in a menu created by the showPlayerChoices function. Point out to the ninja that the string argument in the choice parameter must exactly match (including spelling and capitalization) the string used in the parameter of the showPlayerChoices function. 

💡 When the user makes a choice, a difficulty will be selected based on their response. The number of Person sprites will be increased as the difficulty level is increased. This makes it harder for the Ninja sprite to be found among the Person sprites on screen.
steps.instructions:
Create 3 possible game conditions that will happen as a result of the user’s choice.


Open Logic and drag [if else] under showPlayerChoices. Turn else into an else if condition, then add an else condition to the end of the statement.


Open Story and drag [last answer equals (choice)] inside the parentheses of the if and else if conditions. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

story.checkLastAnswer("")

The checkLastAnswer function takes 1 parameter: choice. Type the string “Easy” inside the parentheses of the if condition, and “Hard” inside the else if condition. 


Inside the curly brackets of all 3 conditions, call the callLevel function and pass the number of Person sprites that should be spawned in each level. Use a smaller number, such as 25, for “Easy” and larger numbers for the other 2 levels.


Click ▶ to see the 3 possible choices being presented to the user, and notice how selecting the different choices changes the number of Person sprites spawned.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use setScale to change the Player sprite’s initial size?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the setScale function used to increase the size of the Player sprite?

❓ Why should the Player sprite be placed in the top right corner of the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that the setScale function assigns the sprite a scale based on the image’s dimension. If the value parameter is greater than 1, the sprite’s size will increase. If it is less than 1, the sprite’s size will decrease. If the scale of a sprite’s image is increased from the middle, the sprite will grow equally from its center. 

💡 The Player sprite should be placed in the top right corner of the screen so that there is a smaller chance that it does not immediately overlap the Ninja sprite.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the game!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] under setBackgroundColor. Use magnifyingGlass as the sprite name, then replace img`...` with the magnifyingGlassImage variable. 


Open Sprites again and drag [set (mySprite) scale to (1) anchor (ScaleAnchor.Middle)] underneath the existing code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name, then change the value parameter from 1 to 1.25 to make the sprite appear slightly larger. Use the default anchor property ScaleAnchor.Middle. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under sprites.create. Update the sprite name, then set the Player sprite to appear at the top right of the screen.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player sprite’s z property so that it appears in front of the Person and Ninja sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might happen when the Player sprite finds the hidden Ninja sprite?

❓ Why is the Player sprite’s z property set to 2?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In the next step, the Ninja sprite’s size will be increased and brought to the center, when the Player sprite overlaps it. 

💡 The Player sprite’s z-position should be set to 2 so that it appears in front of the Ninja and Person sprites on screen.
steps.instructions:
Move the Player sprite to find the hiding Ninja sprite! 


Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the Player sprite’s code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name then adjust the vx and vy parameters so the Player sprite can move in all 4 directions. 


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath the Player sprite movement code. Update the sprite name, then change the flag parameter to SpriteFlag.StayInScreen and the on parameter to true.


Below the Player sprite’s existing code, set the Player sprite’s z-position to 2, so it appears in front of the Person sprites.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite move around on top of the other sprites on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a Boolean variable that gets toggled to true when the Player sprite overlaps with the Ninja sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps the Ninja sprite?

❓ How are the Ninja sprite’s z-position and scale used to display it on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps the Ninja sprite, the ninjaFound variable will be set to true, the Ninja sprite’s z-position will be set to 2, and the Ninja sprite’s scale will be changed by 2. This allows the Ninja sprite to appear in front of the other Person sprites and for its size to increase, making it more obvious on screen. 

💡 Remind the ninja that the changeScale function increases or decreases a sprite’s size by a certain amount. If the value parameter is a positive number, the sprite will grow by that amount multiplied by its current size. If the value parameter is a negative number, the sprite will shrink by that amount multiplied by its current size.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps the Ninja sprite!


Create a Boolean variable to toggle when the Ninja sprite has been found! Under // variable and array set up, declare a ninjaFound variable assigned a value of  false.


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // game events. Change the otherKind parameter to Ninja. 


Inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event, set ninjaFound to true.


Make the Ninja sprite appear on top once it is found. Type otherSprite, then set the z-position to 2, so the Ninja sprite appears in front of the Person sprites. 


Open Sprites and drag [change (mySprite) scale to (1) anchor (ScaleAnchor.Middle)] under the existing code of the onOverlap event. Replace mySprite with otherSprite, then update the value parameter to 2. 


Click ▶ to see the Ninja sprite appear in front and “grow” once the Player sprite finds it.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use spriteMoveToLocation and update all 4 parameters to move the Player sprite to the middle of the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the spriteMoveToLocation function from the Story extension similar and different from the setPosition function from the Sprites menu? 

❓ How is the spriteSayText function from the Story extension similar and different from the sayText function from the Sprites menu?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Explain to the ninja that the setPosition function from the Sprites menu places a sprite at a specific position on screen, based on the submitted x and y-parameters. The spriteMoveToLocation function from the Story extension moves the sprite from its current position to a new position, based on the submitted x and y-parameters. This function makes the movement to the new position visible on screen. 

💡 Explain to the ninja that the sayText function from the Sprites menu displays a speech bubble over the given sprite for a set amount of time. The spriteSayText function from the Story extension is not a speech bubble and the text appears 1 letter at a time. This function will display the text for the duration of its own timer and will pause the rest of the project, until all of the text has been displayed.
steps.instructions:
Use the Story extension to create an ending to the game! 


Open Story, drag [(sprite) move to x (x) y (y) with speed (100)] under the changeScale code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

story.spriteMoveToLocation(sprite, 0, 0, 100)

The spriteMoveToLocation function takes 4 parameters: sprite, x, y, speed. Replace sprite with otherSprite, then adjust the x and y parameters so the Ninja sprite moves to the middle of the screen. Leave the default speed parameter 100.


Open Story, drag [(sprite) say (:))] under the spriteMoveToLocation code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

story.spriteSayText(sprite, ":)")

The spriteSayText function takes 5 parameters: sprite, text, foreground, background, speed. Replace sprite with otherSprite. Update the text parameter with a string that the Ninja sprite has been found. Use commas to add the other parameters to adjust the text and background colors using values between 0-15. Optionally, add a speed parameter too! 


Click ▶ to see the Ninja sprite reveal itself when it is found.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an equality operator to check if the ninjaFound variable is false inside the if condition in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps with a Person sprite?

❓ How is the changeScale function used to make the overlapped Person sprite grow then shrink?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps with a Person sprite, if the the ninjaFound variable is false, the Person sprite will grow, the project will pause briefly, then the Person sprite will shrink back to its regular size. This mimics what would happen if a real magnifying glass was used to scan a set of items.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps with the Person sprites.


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath the Player/ Ninja onOverlap event. Change the otherKind parameter to Person. 


Open Logic and drag [if] inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event. Inside the if condition, check if the ninjaFound variable is false. 


Make the Person sprites “grow” on overlap with the Player sprite. Open Sprites and drag [change (mySprite) scale to (1) anchor (ScaleAnchor.Middle)] inside the curly brackets of the if conditional. Replace mySprite with otherSprite then use the default value parameter 1 and anchor property ScaleAnchor.Middle. 


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] below the changeScale code. Set the parameter so that the project pauses briefly after the Person sprite grows.


Copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) the changeScale code under pause. Update the parameter to -1 so the Person sprite “shrinks” back to normal.


Click ▶ to see each Person sprite grow then shrink as the Player sprite overlaps them.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a startCountdown inside the callLevel function definition and a stopCountdown inside the Player/Ninja onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How long might the user have to find the Ninja sprite?

❓ What does the stopCountdown function do? How is it used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to set the countdown duration parameter to a reasonable amount of time so that the game is challenging, but not impossible.

💡 The stopCountdown function stops the current countdown and hides the countdown display. Without using this function, the game would not end when the Ninja sprite is found. 

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the  setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Add a countdown timer to the game! 


Open Info and drag [start countdown (10) (s)] inside the callLevel function. Update the duration parameter to set how long the user has to find the Ninja sprite. 


Open Info and drag [stop countdown] into the Player/Ninja onOverlap event.


Open Game and drag [game over (true)] below the spriteSayText code inside the Player/Ninja onOverlap event. Change the win parameter to true and add an effect, too.


Click ▶ to see the countdown timer begin after the user selects the challenge level!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add showLongText to the beginning of the project and inside the curly brackets of the callLevel function to prepare the user for the project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What title or directions might tell the user what the project is about or how to play? 

❓ What frame might be used to display each dialog box?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding directions to the project!


Open Game and drag [set dialog frame to (frame)] underneath the setBackgroundColor code under // game set up. Select a dialog frame image from the gallery.


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath the setDialogFrame code. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box introduces the project’s task and lets the user know that they will be choosing their level difficulty. 


Open Game and drag another [show long text (str) (layout)] inside the curly brackets of the callLevel function on top of the existing code. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box informs the user that the timer is about to start. 


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses the Story extension to offer different choices to the user and create different outcomes depending on their choice!

validationItems.text: Create a personList image array and set the background color.
Create a callLevel function and use a documentation comment.
Inside the callLevel function, create a Ninja sprite and set its position.
Inside the callLevel function, use a for loop to create multiple Person sprites.
Use the Story extension to create different levels of difficulty.
Add a Player sprite using the magnifyingGlassImage variable, set its scale, set its position, move it with the controller, make it stay in the screen, and place it on top of other sprites.
Use an onOverlap event and a Boolean toggle to track when the Ninja sprite is found. Change the scale of the otherSprite and make it appear on top of other sprites.
Use the Story extension to have the ninja sprite move and say text.
Use an onOverlap event to make the Person sprites get larger when they overlap with the Player sprite.
Add a countdown timer and game over logic.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 6 of Purple Belt! Before you create your final Purple Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 6:

badges.title: Extension Explorer
badges.description: Use animation and music code, plus the scroller and story extensions, to enhance a project.

badges.title: Stop Motion
badges.description: Use an array of images to create an animation for a sprite.

badges.title: Path of Least Resistance
badges.description: Use an animation preset path to animate a sprite’s movement.

badges.title: Earworm
badges.description: Create a custom melody using a string of note names.

badges.title: Seven Layer Dip
badges.description: Use the Scroller extension to change the background image layers.

badges.title: Parallax Party
badges.description: Use the Scroller extension to move a background layer to create a parallax effect.

badges.title: The Choice is Yours
badges.description: Use the Story extension to present the player with choices.

badges.title: Stage Directions
badges.description: Use the Story extension to move a sprite to a specific position.

badges.title: What’s my Line?
badges.description: Use the Story extension to have a sprite say text with custom colors.
